attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post, written in his voice as an aside. He is not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: Turning 'so many of the unfortunate consequences' into 'many of the harmful consequences' keeps the scope. The statement is unhedged and describes the present state, so it is correctly an observation.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: several documented harms fall unequally on women or minority groups, without every harm having to hit every group. The speaker gave no measure, so the reading decides the result. Limiting evidence to audits from before the post fits the observation.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed C4 audit from 2021, before the post. The blocklist removed African American and Hispanic-aligned English far more often than White-aligned English. Dialect stands in for author identity, but the group comparison is clear.

2021 LAION-400M audit. Ordinary feminine and minority-woman search terms returned sexualized results. This is exploratory and does not measure prevalence, but it documents a group-linked representational harm.

2021 CLIP probes. Black images were misclassified as non-human at about 14%, against under 8% for every other group. One qualification: crime-term misclassification hit male images more than female ones. That limits any claim that every harm falls on women, but it does not reverse the overall pattern.

reviews.rationale: Three original audits from before the post document several group-linked harms: minority dialects excluded from a web corpus, sexualized retrieval for women's terms in LAION, and racial denigration in CLIP. The one counter-finding (men misclassified more often for crime terms) concerns a single harm and a single group. It does not meet the contradiction condition, which requires disparities to be absent or reversed across the relevant harms. So under the fair plain reading, the claim is supported.
